Mythic Wonders: The Philosopher's Stone, developed by Organic 2 Digital Studio and published by Artifex Mundi, is a hidden object adventure game that immerses players in a magical and mysterious world filled with puzzles, secrets, and enchanting visuals. The game follows Emma, a young woman who becomes concerned for her uncle Alfred after experiencing unsettling dreams about him. Upon visiting his apartment, she discovers that a portal project they had been collaborating on has inadvertently opened a gateway to a mythical realm. This sets the stage for a journey through fantastical landscapes where Emma must rescue her uncle and uncover the secrets surrounding the legendary Philosopher’s Stone. The narrative is rich with fantasy elements, combining a sense of adventure with a mysterious storyline that keeps players engaged throughout.

Gameplay in Mythic Wonders is centered on classic hidden object mechanics. Players are tasked with locating a variety of items scattered throughout intricately detailed scenes. Each area is thoughtfully designed, challenging players’ observational skills while simultaneously encouraging exploration of the environment. These hidden object segments are interspersed with logic-based puzzles and mini-games, which provide additional challenges that test problem-solving abilities. The balance of hidden object scenes and puzzles ensures that gameplay remains varied and engaging, appealing to both newcomers to the genre and experienced players seeking a casual yet rewarding adventure.

The visual presentation of the game is one of its most striking features. The hand-drawn environments are vibrant and meticulously crafted, capturing the whimsical and magical nature of the mythical world Emma explores. Character designs are expressive, and the backgrounds are rich with detail, enhancing the sense of immersion. The aesthetic choices, from color palettes to lighting effects, work together to create a visually enchanting experience that complements the game’s narrative and gameplay. The combination of lush environments and engaging art style makes exploration particularly satisfying, as players uncover hidden items and secrets within the beautifully crafted scenes.

Audio design in Mythic Wonders further enhances the experience. A melodic and atmospheric soundtrack accompanies the gameplay, creating a sense of wonder and tension that aligns with the narrative’s magical and mysterious tone. Sound effects, such as subtle environmental noises or audio cues during puzzles, help guide players and heighten engagement. The lack of intrusive or overly dramatic music allows the player to focus on the story and the discovery process, maintaining a relaxing yet immersive experience.

The Collector’s Edition of the game adds even more depth, including a bonus chapter titled “The Origins of the Guardian,” which expands on the lore of the game and provides additional puzzles and challenges. Collectible items and morphing objects throughout the game encourage players to explore thoroughly and revisit areas to uncover all secrets, adding replayability and rewarding careful observation. These features enhance the overall value of the game and provide extra content for those who enjoy fully immersing themselves in the game world.

In conclusion, Mythic Wonders: The Philosopher's Stone is a captivating hidden object adventure that combines a compelling story, intricate puzzles, and enchanting visuals. Its accessible yet engaging gameplay, paired with a richly detailed mythical world, makes it an ideal choice for players seeking a relaxing and immersive experience. Whether you are a longtime fan of hidden object games or new to the genre, the title offers a thoughtfully crafted journey full of magic, mystery, and discovery.

[u]Recommendation[/u]: A decent hidden object game that avoids most of the pitfalls present in many previous Artifex Mundi games.

[u]Critique[/u]: This game should be called "Mythic Wonders: Something is Missing Here" instead, because you will [i]constantly[/i] get the message "Something is missing here" throughout the game (I'm not kidding - if you see this message much fewer than 50 times in the game, I'll be very much surprised).

Does this have a completely bonkers story? 
Yes. (But it's entertaining.)
Does it have howlingly bad CGI for the cut scenes?
Absolutely. (But it's better than a lot of the others.)
Does it have illogical solutions to puzzles that ignore other items that would work better in your inventory?
Sure. (But they're very, very consistent AND sometimes you will actually [i]keep a tool[/i] to use again later!!!!)

There are some irritating things that are blissfully absent in this game:
- there's no instances of the wrong word being used to describe an object
- there's no coin being used as a screwdriver (amazing!!!)
- there's no alternative minigame requiring you play through the game a second time to get all the achievements
- there isn't a huge list of alternative hidden objects that you have to find to accomplish secondary objectives (sadly, there ARE morphing items that you have to find, but they're very obvious, and there's only a few of them)
- nobody is kidnapped or held hostage

Most astonishing of all, I don't think there are any crows in this game. Is this a first for Artifex Mundi???!?

What this means is that you have a fairly run-of-the-mill hidden object game that feels just slightly better than others, because of a bunch of little quality of life improvements. Instead of a buddy that helps you fetch items you can't reach (as in so many previous games), in [u]Mythic Wonders[/u], you get a magical device that allows you to alter your environment to reveal objects you couldn't access otherwise. Mechanically, it's almost the same, but narratively, I like it a lot better.

[u]Review[/u]: You play as Emma, a young woman in 1930s Europe who has been helping her uncle with constructing a contraption. She's gone home, but as the game begins, she is returning to rejoin her uncle in the laboratory. [spoiler]Upon arrival, she finds that her uncle has completed the construction of the portal and has gone through it. A guardian spirit appears to waylay her throughout her journey to be reunited with her family member. This journey takes her to different elemental realms where she must both: 
- reassemble devices to power up the portals in each of these worlds so she can leave
- find and assimilate the elemental essence of that realm into a device called "the Philosopher's Stone"

As the story continues, it becomes clear that her uncle is a bad guy who desires the ability of the Philosopher's Stone to control the elements for his own selfish purposes. But it requires someone "pure of heart" to assemble it, so that's where Emma comes in. The spirit guardian (as we discover in the Bonus Chapter prologue to the main game) was actually created by their ancestors to prevent the Philosopher's Stone from ever being reassembled. In the end, Emma completes the Philosopher's Stone, the guardian banishes her uncle, and she relinquishes the artifact to the guardian once more.[/spoiler]

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Insomma, un gioco veramente brutto, non al punto da essere ingiocabile, per carità, ma sinceramente c'è di molto meglio in giro per gli appassionati del genere.

Standard Artifex Mundi HOG: overpriced except when on sale, but works well as a casual timekiller. Of note, this one actually had some challenging HO scenes and you'll need the Info button to figure out what you're supposed to do with a few puzzles.

As usual, my comments below are relative to the typical quality level of HOGs, not AAA games.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
+Multiple difficulties
+Colorful, well-animated and rather detailed
+Save anywhere with multiple player profiles
+Hints and puzzle skips available
+Map with points of interest is nice
+Journal holds pictures of clues
+In-game achievement tracker
+Bonus chapter

[h1]YMMV[/h1]
~Voice acting is occasionally cringey, even for a HOG
~Morphing charms achievement is easily missable
~One particular document had a bunch of typos
~Many items are indistinguishable from detailed backgrounds
~A few unclear puzzles
~Roughly 4 hours of playtime. Less if you play on Normal difficulty, where the game treats you like a complete cretin, pointing out all the items you didn't select in less than a minute.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
-A few pictorial HO lists are hard to interpret (the valve one comes to mind)
-"Goes before" does not necessarily mean "immediately precedes"

This HOG was all right but definitely has its fair share of flaws.

Story: 3/5
The basic concept is intriguing: Find your uncle by traveling to different worlds using a series of magic portals. Each world had its own theme: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Aether. I think Air may have been the most striking because of all the tinted glass, in my opinion. 

I was enjoying visiting each world but it did grow stale after a while. Each world got larger and required more tasks to complete, but it felt monotonous after a while. The final battle is also way too easy, and the ending feels rushed. Lastly, the Guardian was terrible at his job because he made weak threats and put obstacles in my way that weren't challenging to overcome. 

Graphics: 3.5/5
The visuals in this game are a mixed bag: Character designs and animations are great but they don't move their mouths when talking. Each world has its own theme and is quite detailed, but the quality seemed lower than that of other games I've played. Some parts of areas in the beginning were rather bland while others were quite lovely and vibrant. Pretty much all the cut scene animations were blurry. I mean, the game still looks relatively good, but the quality is definitely not up to par with what I'm used to seeing in these games -- and this one isn't even that old. 

Music: 3.5/5
It's pretty, and each world has its own fitting music, but most of it is generic. I like it but just don't find it to be all that memorable.

Voice Acting: 2/5
Quite bad, honestly. The main character sounds so wooden whenever she speaks. The only character with decent voice acting was the Guardian -- but even he still could have been better. The bad voice acting may have had a lot to do with my growing disinterest with the story the more I progressed.

Hidden Object Puzzles: 4.5/5
There was a mix of the standard "find items from the list" scenes, but also some where you had to find all instances of a particular item or finding items based on images in a list as opposed to words. Nothing ground-breaking but the variety was appreciated. My only complaint is that some of the HOG scenes were a little blurry in some spots.

Other Puzzles: 3.5/5
Not bad for the most part. Some were fun, such as untangling octopus tentacles (how stretchy!) and deciphering the correct order of runes for each portal based on abstract clues. But others were annoying or just plain ridiculous. Like, trying to fly the air ship in the Wind World was very confusing and frustrating. I couldn't figure out the "method," which is normally an easy enough tasks in other games with something similar. 

 Overall rating: 67%
It's worth playing for the hidden object scenes and the unique worlds you visit, but I'd definitely wait until it's on sale.

So, this is a weird one to write. Mostly, I don't have an issue with the game. I found it to be charming and vaguely reminiscent of Demon Hunter: Chronicles from Beyond. The different worlds were all fine, the hidden object games actually have some quality of life improvements to them I wish the rest of the games had; if you're picking one of the compound hidden objects, like say there's a message in a bottle and you need to break the bottle open to get it, in this game, when you use the hammer, it automatically collects the message instead of making you do the extra step of clicking again. I appreciated that.

There are collectibles and a bonus adventure too, and a lot of those sounds an animations were very well done.

Mostly my gripe with this is, several of the puzzles were broken / followed no logic, and the collectibles were all transforming objects but a lot of them never transformed to indicate they were collectibles. These were both annoying. The puzzles, not all of them were broken, but for example there's a puzzle to bounce around colored beams of light. The light travels through these 'L' and 'T' shaped junctions. Sometimes passing the light beam through it would make it come out all of the other sides of that junction, and sometimes it just didn't... No clear reason as to why, and it really upsets me when games have puzzles and they puzzles don't follow consistent logic. There were a few other ones that didn't seem to work very well or ones that seemed to require outside information not found in the game to complete. I also use a tablet, so having to play on expert difficulty for one of the achievements I also didn't like. It hides the hidden object puzzle prompts that I can't use a cursor to find, since on a tablet, there is no cursor unless you use the trackpad.

So, you might have better luck if you don't mind skipping some sections and don't mind not getting achievements, but if not, this might bother you too.

Un "point and click" vraiment sympathique, qui verse dans la Low Fantasy / Fantastique, sans grande prise de tête et ça se voit et sent. On navigue entre une demi-dizaine de tableaux bien fournis à la recherche d'éléments à collecter, de mini-jeux à essayer et d'énigmes à résoudre ; énigmes qui, pour certaines, peuvent étonnement surprendre quand on voit le gabarit de ce jeu (dès lors même quand on connaît le gabarit de ce style de jeu).

Côté histoire, bon... Il n'y a pas grand chose à dire, c'est quelque peu tiré par les cheveux et il ne faut pas s'attendre à avoir d'énormes explications concernant l'intrigue qui nous est offerte. Néanmoins, on se prend tout de même de l'aventure au côté de notre héroïne, alors quelque part, le "pari" est réussi. C'est notamment, et surtout, comme j'ai pu le déclarer précédemment, dans les énigmes à résoudre que l'on va trouver son compte (si on ne s'amuse pas à passer ces dernières, auquel cas le jeu est très très rapide à être bouclé).

Les séquences cinématographiques sont sympathiques malgré la rigidité des personnes et la chute remarquable (dans le sens où on le remarque hein) de qualité.

En bref, c'est un jeu sans grande prétention, plutôt divertissant qui se termine assez rapidement et qui occupe l'esprit le temps d'un voyage ou d'une attente de téléchargement/installation d'un autre jeu.
Point and click varié: objets cachés, puzzles, assemblages d'objets. Jeu très facile pour les habitués, mais parfait pour  les enfants (ou bien pour ceux qui veulent un  jeu très light).
